title: Short Stuff: Blaschko's Lines
summary: Short Stuff episode on Blaschko's lines, the faint striped patterns present on all human skin that are visible under UV/black light. The hosts explain they were named after dermatologist Alfred Blaschko, who first described them around 1901, and that they do not follow blood vessels or nerves. The leading explanation is that they mark migration routes of skin cells during fetal development, with humans described as genetic mosaics. The episode compares this to identical twins and chimerism, mentions Max Scherzer's two-colored eyes, describes general patterns on the body (V shape on the back, wave shape on the trunk, S shape on the abdomen, spirals on the scalp), notes that teeth, eyes and tongue also have them, and covers conditions such as vitiligo and hyperpigmentation that make the lines visible in normal light. The episode opens with a tour-date reminder for Pacific Northwest shows in February.

segments.title: Introduction to human striped skin
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the idea that humans are a striped species, visible only under UV light, and name the topic Blaschko's lines.

segments.title: Origin of the name and the migration theory
segments.summary: Blaschko's lines were named after dermatologist Alfred Blaschko, who described them around 1901. They do not follow blood vessels or nerves. The leading idea is that they are traces of skin cell migration during fetal development, with a Mental Floss description quoted.

segments.title: Why the lines are visible: mosaicism and chimerism
segments.summary: Skin cells are nearly identical genetically but differ slightly due to experiences during development, making humans genetic mosaics. The hosts compare this to identical twins, mention epigenetics and Doppelgangers, and contrast mosaicism with chimerism, including two-colored eyes such as Max Scherzer's.

segments.title: Patterns on the body and other body parts
segments.summary: The lines follow general patterns such as a V shape on the back, a wave shape on the trunk, an S shape on the abdomen, and spirals on the scalp. Teeth, eyes and tongue also have them.

segments.title: Conditions that reveal the lines
segments.summary: Conditions such as vitiligo can follow the lines as pigment loss, and some congenital hyperpigmentation makes them visible in normal light, like tiger stripes.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and thank listeners.
